question: A study,1 the first of its kind, has made public its findings concerning the repercussions of climate change for monuments belonging to the cultural heritage of Greece. While the study centred on three sites in Greece, its findings are applicable more broadly to the rest of Europe, and especially to the Mediterranean countries, such as Cyprus.

The study warns that the combination of rising temperatures and higher levels of atmospheric humidity in summer will lead to many of Greece’s celebrated archaeological sites, museum exhibits and monuments deteriorating faster than expected. This, the report says, is due to the way in which the changing climate alters the chemical composition of the materials used at the sites and in the works of art concerned.

This will cause mould to develop and accelerate the disintegration of building materials. We must make every effort to protect our historical sites and monuments from repercussions of any kind. In view of the above, what steps does the Commission propose to take to protect the most valuable historical monuments on our continent from climate change and avert their further degradation?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.3.2024) European cultural heritage is supported by a range of EU policies, programmes, and funding. The European Framework for Action on Cultural Heritage1 provides a common approach to heritage-related activities at European level.

The Commission also recognises the need to protect and preserve cultural heritage specifically from climate change impacts, including in the EU Strategy on Adaptation to Climate Change2. The most effective way to protect cultural heritage monuments is to arrest global warming, but steps also must be taken to build resilience to the impacts already underway.

The Commission supports Member States to do so through a variety of means. Horizon Europe, the programme for research and innovation3, funds projects designed to increase resilience and rebuild historic areas sustainably. The culture strand of Creative Europe programme4 supports the preservation of cultural heritage, including resilience to changing climate conditions.

The EU Floods Directive5 requires Member States to report regularly on their cultural heritage sites that might be affected by flooding. The EU Civil Protection Mechanism6 is meant to safeguard not only human life, but also the environment and property, including cultural heritage.

The Copernicus7 programme, designed to support Member States in managing natural and non-natural geohazards can detect potential impacts in cultural heritage sites. The Work Plan for Culture 2019-2022 established an Open Method of Coordination group of experts on strengthening cultural heritage resilience to climate change.
The group identified examples of cultural heritage solutions in the context of climate change from 26 countries.8
